references.cited_as: Johnson KM, et al. Open Forum Infect Dis 2019;6(9):ofz393
references.record_title: Comparison of Diagnosis and Prescribing Practices Between Virtual Visits and Office Visits for Adults Diagnosed With Sinusitis Within a Primary Care Network.

claims.text: 350 adults in one primary care network, 175 per group; retrospective cohort
claims.quote: This retrospective cohort study evaluated adult patients diagnosed with sinusitis treated within a single primary care network. ... A total of 350 patients were included in the study, with 175 in each group.

claims.text: Guideline-concordant diagnosis 69.1% virtual vs 45.7% office, P<.001
claims.quote: Patients treated for sinusitis were more likely to receive a guideline-concordant diagnosis in the virtual visit group (69.1% vs 45.7%;< .001).

claims.text: Fewer virtual patients received antibiotics, 68.6% vs 94.3%, P<.001
claims.quote: patients who completed virtual visits were less likely to receive antibiotics (68.6% vs 94.3%;< .001).

claims.text: Guideline-concordant drug selection similar, 67.5% vs 64.8%
claims.quote: Guideline-concordant antibiotic selection was similar between groups (67.5% vs 64.8%;= .641).

claims.text: Virtual patients more likely to revisit within 24 hours (8% vs 1.7%) and 30 days (14.9% vs 7.4%)
claims.quote: Patients completing virtual visits were more likely to revisit for sinusitis within 24 hours (8% vs 1.7%;= .006) and within 30 days (14.9% vs 7.4%;= .027).

claims.text: Association only (retrospective design); virtual care associated with better diagnosis and less prescribing
claims.quote: care at a virtual visit was associated with an increase in guideline-concordant diagnosis and a decrease in antibiotic prescribing compared with in-person primary care visits.

claims.text: For sinusitis, virtual visits led to antibiotics less often (closing summary, with refs 2 and 4)
claims.quote: patients who completed virtual visits were less likely to receive antibiotics (68.6% vs 94.3%;< .001).

claims.text: Overall prescribing lower virtual 72.1% vs 76.7%; OR 0.783, P<.001
claims.quote: There was a statistically significant lower rate of antibiotic prescriptions for ARS in 2020 (72.1%) versus 2019 (76.7%).The odds ratio for an antibiotic prescription for ARS was 0.783 (95% confidence interval, 0.693-0.86; P < .001)

claims.text: No significant difference among otolaryngology providers (P=.781)
claims.quote: When stratified by otolaryngology providers there was no statistically significant difference of antibiotic prescriptions between the 2019 and 2020 cohort (P = .781).

claims.text: Telemedicine did not increase antibiotic prescribing despite no physical exam
claims.quote: telemedicine did not result in an increase in antibiotic prescribing despite the lack of an in-person physical exam.

claims.text: FAQ JSON-LD: 5,729 visits, lower virtual rate, no OTO difference
claims.quote: There was a statistically significant lower rate of antibiotic prescriptions for ARS in 2020 (72.1%) versus 2019 (76.7%).
